progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b09: biotechnology spans agriculture, medicine and industry; insulin came from pig and cattle pancreases from 1922 and from bacteria from 1982; chymosin for cheese, once from calves' stomachs, is now mostly made by microbes. From b18: how DNA for human insulin is put into bacteria, which make insulin chains in large fermenters; chymosin bacteria (attempt 1). From b10: judgements name who gains and who carries the risk. From b11: CRISPR cuts chosen DNA; working in a trial is not the same as proven or available. From b12: biodiversity has genetic, species and ecosystem levels; an effect is a change from a baseline; one variety everywhere narrows a crop's genetic diversity. From b13: Bt cotton cut insecticide use by about 85 per cent compared with conventional cotton; refuges slow resistance; verdicts carry a condition. From bio-m5-b06c: genes code for proteins as amino acid sequences. From skills-s04: evaluate means judge against criteria with evidence. Not assumed: the papaya case, the animal and human insulin trial comparison, the growth hormone history, sperm washing, germline editing's specific case.
progression.startsWith: Compare agricultural, medical and industrial cases. The video opens: In 1982, human insulin made by bacteria was approved, and it's now used around the world.
progression.stopsAfter: stating that a benefit must be better than an alternative, shown by evidence and received by someone, and testing a claim with "Better than what? Shown how? Who gets it?"; explaining why the 2018 embryo edit fails all three (an existing method already protected the embryos, and HIV can be prevented in other ways later in life; the edits were untested and did not copy the natural protective variant; the children carried the risk without consent); evaluating virus-resistant papaya (no ordinary variety resisted the virus; harvests climbed back after 1998, to about three quarters of the earlier level by 2001; growers gained); evaluating recombinant insulin (it controls blood sugar about as well as purified pig insulin for most patients, so its clear benefit is a reliable, scalable supply; access depends on price); explaining why recombinant growth hormone's benefit is larger (the old pituitary source was scarce and some batches spread a fatal brain disease); evaluating microbe-made chymosin (the same enzyme without depending on calves); explaining why agriculture is the most contested domain (organisms are released, so pests evolve and crop genetic diversity can narrow; Bt cotton's benefit holds while refuges keep resistance rare); ranking benefits by irreplaceability, evidence and reach rather than by how advanced the technology is (growth hormone and the papaya far better than what came before, with clear evidence; insulin and chymosin clear on supply; growth hormone's and insulin's reach depend on cost); applying this to an unseen assess item and an unseen evaluate item.
progression.nextLesson: practice questions that weigh benefits against biodiversity and ethics (route entry bio-m6-g02), then why social context can limit long-term genetic change (bio-m6-b20).

teaching.task: Bacteria making insulin and an edited human embryo both used genetic technology to promise a health benefit, yet one is accepted worldwide and the other was condemned. So which benefits of genetic technology actually hold up, and how can you tell?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why a benefit needs a comparison (a benefit is a difference from what came before, 2); why the embryo edit fails (an existing method already protected the embryos and HIV can be prevented in other ways later in life; untested edits; risk without consent, 2); why the papaya benefit is strong (no alternative worked; harvests climbed back, 3); why insulin's benefit is supply rather than effect (pig insulin worked about as well in trials; the old supply depended on abattoirs, 4); why growth hormone's benefit is bigger (the old source was scarce and some batches carried a fatal disease, 5); why chymosin holds up (the same enzyme without calves, 6; fungal enzymes' bitterness is a screen tag); why agriculture is most contested (released organisms meet wild species, pests evolve, one variety narrows diversity, 7); why the ranking falls as it does (irreplaceability, real-outcome evidence, reach; scene 8 claims only what the board shows: growth hormone's and the papaya's first two cells, with growth hormone's reach left open as "depends on cost", 8). Visible case: the dying and healthy papaya pair, the bead strips with one and three differences, the equal trial bars, the supply line thickening, the matching enzyme glyphs, the sealed tank beside the open field. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items. Reading load: at most about three bright text items; the board cells are two to four words.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Bacteria-made insulin and an edited human embryo both promised a health benefit, yet one is accepted worldwide and the other was condemned, so the question is which benefits of genetic technology hold up and how to tell. A benefit is always better than something, shown by evidence, for someone, so three tests (better than what, shown how, who gets it) are tried on the embryo edit and then applied across the BenefitBoard: virus-resistant papaya on the farm, insulin and growth hormone in medicine (where the old source was scarce, impure or dangerous), and chymosin in industry; tank or field explains why farm uses are argued over most (the modified organism is released), and the ranking shows benefits are strongest where the technology did something the old method could not do safely and the evidence measures the real outcome. A gain in harvest is not a gain in biodiversity. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: In 1982, human insulin made by bacteria was approved, and it's now used around the world. In 2018, a researcher edited a gene in human embryos, hoping twin girls would resist HIV. Scientists everywhere condemned it, and he was sent to prison. Both used genetic technology, and both promised a health benefit. So that label alone can't tell you which one to trust. Which benefits actually hold up, and how can you tell?
teaching.understandingCheck: 10a is an assess item: laundry enzymes from modified microbes clean at 20 °C; most of a wash's energy heats the water; assess the company's claim that its enzymes cut household energy use. It tests "shown how?" (the benefit happens only if people wash cold). 10c is an evaluate item: the plasma-derived hepatitis B vaccine (1981) against the yeast-made vaccine (1986), both protective; evaluate the yeast vaccine's benefit. It transfers scene 4's insight (when the old product worked, the benefit is supply and safety). Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the full card stays on screen during and after the countdown. Each feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s): the answer, the key reason, the givens underlined in the question strip as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: B6-IQ3-05: "evaluate the benefits of using genetic technologies in agricultural, medical and industrial applications (ACSBL086)". This video owns first coverage of B6-IQ3-05. It also touches B6-IQ2-01's example "evaluating the potential benefits for society of research using genetic technologies" (scene 2 and the attempts), shared with b11 and g02. Update the ledger rows when this design passes review. The verb "evaluate" (skills-s04: make a judgement and support it with relevant criteria and evidence) is carried by the three tests (the criteria), each case's evidence, the ranking verdict (scene 8) and attempt 2; "assess" (how far, how much) by attempt 1.

design.visualSystem: One benefit board: a coded three-by-three grid, columns "farm", "medicine", "industry" (each headed by a small painted thumbnail), rows "Better than what?", "Shown how?", "Who gets it?". Each case scene opens its column large in the main stage (the board shrinks to the upper right), and each test answer writes into its cell as a two to four word chip with a coloured strength dot (amber filled: holds up strongly; amber half: partly; grey ring: not shown). Finished cells dim to grey. Scene 8 enlarges the whole board for the ranking. Painted plates for real things: `m6-insulin-vial-v1.png`, `m6-icsi-v1.png` (the injected egg; hook and scene 2), new `m6-papaya-healthy-v1.png` and `m6-papaya-ringspot-v1.png` (an aligned pair, scene 3), `m8-pancreas-v1.png` (scene 4), `m6-bacterium-plasmid-v1.png` (hook, scene 5), new `m6-fermenter-tank-v1.png` (scenes 4 and 7; requested by b18), new `m6-growth-hormone-vial-v1.png` (scene 5), `m6-dairy-calf-horn-buds-v1.png` (scene 6, the calf, small), new `m6-cheese-wheel-v1.png` (scene 6), `m6-bt-cotton-v1.png` and `m6-field-monoculture-mixed-v1.png` (scene 7), new `m6-washing-machine-v1.png` (attempt 1), `y11-budding-yeast-v1.png` and `m7-vaccine-vial-syringe-v1.png` (attempt 2). Coded: the board, chips, strength dots, the amino acid bead strips, the trial bar pair, the supply line, the tank and field outlines, the arrows. No people, no hands, no faces. The twins, the researcher and patients are never drawn; the embryo case is shown only by the injected-egg plate and chips. Never used: `m6-hand-pollination-v1.png` and `m6-agricultural-liming-v1.png` (retired hand plates). Plates scale proportionally, never stretched. Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): at most about three bright text items at once besides the small grey board labels; each tag fades when the next cue lands; filled cells dim.
design.transitionPlan: The bacterium and insulin vial plates open the hook, joined by the injected egg plate with its grey "condemned" chip and a bracket that dims to a "?"; the heading splits into three test chips that settle as row labels down the empty BenefitBoard and are tried on the embryo case; the farm column opens large with the papaya plates and its three cells fill; the medicine column opens with the pancreas plate and insulin, then the growth hormone vial; the industry column opens with the fermenter tank and chymosin; the board shrinks as the tank-or-field contrast draws; the BenefitBoard enlarges with all cells dimmed and the strongest light for the ranking; the three questions write large with icons; each attempt clears the board and its feedback underlines the card as an AnsTable or three rows fill; the decision rule chips and next chip close; scene crossfade with settle.
